HEADLINE: No contest as One Nation won't be distracted by Joyce sideshow
TEXT:
Barnaby Joyce is set to bag an easy victory in the New England byelection after One Nation and the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers Party said they would not field candidates.

One Nation will concentrate its efforts on Queensland rather than be distracted by the "New England sideshow", Pauline Hanson said.

"So it looks like Barnaby Joyce has finally had a little bit of luck go his way," she said via social media.

In a statement, the Shooters Party said it had not made any preparations to field a candidate because "just like the rest of Australia, we believed Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull and Deputy Prime Minister Barnaby Joyce when they stood in Parliament hand on heart, saying that Mr Joyce was not ineligible on the basis of his citizenship".

With Tony Windsor also out of the race, Mr Joyce appears to have a clear run to victory on December 2. Mr Windsor said he believed other serious contenders might step forward but none had so far materialised. Nominations close on November 11.

Despite confirming no presence in the byelection, Shooters Party spokesman Robert Brown took a swipe at the Nationals over their "behaviour" in the Cootamundra and Murray NSW byelections.

"We call on Barnaby Joyce to publicly apologise for allowing his New South Wales party leader John Barilaro to brand licensed firearms owners as extremists," Mr Brown said in a statement.

"Those 12,319 licensed firearms owners - including Mr Joyce himself - do not deserve to be branded as criminals-in-waiting by a desperate National Party in search of a headline. That's 11 per cent of the New England electorate who were personally attacked for undertaking a lawful pursuit."

Shooters candidate Philip Donato won the NSW state byelection in Orange in late 2016 and the party put in a strong showing against Nationals candidates in both the Cootamundra and Murray byelections in mid-October.

Senator Hanson said the party would like to have challenged Mr Joyce but could not be distracted.

"While One Nation is a major threat to the tired old parties and I would love to have seen a One Nation candidate run, it would have been unfair to our hardworking Queensland candidates to have the party become distracted by the New England sideshow."

Confirmed challengers in New England are Ian Britza, a former Liberal member of the WA Legislative Assembly and Rob Taber, who ran as an independent in the 2016 federal election.

HEADLINE: Small business tempted by minor parties
TEXT:
Queensland businesses have threatened to vote for the minor parties, including One Nation, unless there are more policies to kick-start the economy such as boosting infrastructure spending to create jobs.

With Opposition Leader Tim Nicholls pledging to reduce the payroll tax burden and create 500,000 jobs over a decade, business has called for stable government after the November 25 poll.

But this may be wishful thinking, with polls showing a hung parliament or an alliance between the LNP and One Nation could be a real possibility.

While disenchanted voters have been tempted away from the ALP and LNP, peak business body the Chamber of Commerce and Industry Queensland said its small business members were doing likewise.

A recent CCIQ and ReachTEL survey of 1500 businesses found more than a third would vote for a minor party at the state election.

"The small business community is currently split in Queensland with both major parties losing a significant share of votes to Independents, One Nation and the Greens," CCIQ general manager advocacy Kate Whittle said.

"It means that now, more than ever, Labor and the LNP must address the issues important to business with meaningful policies that will help them grow and employ."

On his first full day on the hustings, Mr Nicholls announced payroll tax reform as well as an aspirational pledge to create 500,000 jobs over the next 10 years.

Mr Nicholls said an LNP government would increase the threshold after which businesses had to pay payroll tax by $25,000 every year for the next 10 years to $1.35 million in total taxable wages.

He said this would help more than 14,000 businesses grow without being slugged with a substantially bigger tax bill.

"Businesses should not be discouraged from employing more Queenslanders because of the threat of payroll tax - a tax on jobs," he said.

"It will also mean employers can give workers a well-earned wages increase without worrying about a big payroll tax slug.

"This is especially important because wages growth under Labor has been the worst in the nation."

He said the 500,000 jobs target was based on current economic growth rates.

Employment Minister Grace Grace said Queensland already had the lowest payroll tax rate and highest tax-free threshold in the nation.

She said the LNP job pledge was a bit rich considering Mr Nicholls cut 14,000 public service jobs when he was part of the Newman government in 2012.

Property Council of Australia's Queensland director Chris Mountford said any future government needed to release more land for development.

"It's less about who is in charge and more about what they do. We are keen to see them unlock more activity," Mr Mountford said.

Brisbane-based economist Nick Behrens, who is the director at Queensland Economic Advocacy Solutions, said the business community had found the Palaszczuk government uninspiring.

He said any rebound in economic activity had little to do with the policies of the Labor minority government, saying infrastructure spending had fallen to record lows - partly because the Palaszczuk government was cash-strapped after ruling out asset sales.

"The fiscal performance of the state government has been very disappointing. It has just shifted debt from consolidated revenue to government-owned corporations," he said.

"Infrastructure spending is at historic lows with under-investment to the tune of $6 billion a year. This has provided significant challenges for civil engineering firms."

Key points

Nicholls announces an aim to create 500,000 jobs over the next 10 years.

The Chamber of Commerce says its members are tempted away from the ALP and LNP.

HEADLINE: PM told don't cross Qld's Gympie Line
TEXT:
Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull and Opposition Leader Bill Shorten plan to spend some time in Queensland trying to help their parties ahead of the November 25 state election.

But while Mr Shorten is expected to roam far and wide, including into so-called One Nation territory in north and central Queensland, the Prime Minister, who personally does not resonate well in these regions, is likely to be confined beneath what has been coined the Gympie Line.

A Coalition strategist said should Mr Turnbull visit, as he intends to do, he would be confined mostly to Brisbane, the Gold Coast to the south, and the Sunshine Coast to the immediate north of the state capital. Other than a possible long hop to Cairns, he would be unlikely to roam further north than Gympie.

The Prime Minister's opportunities will be limited, He will miss the first week of the campaign because he is in Israel, and another week when he travels through Asia for annual regional summits, APEC and ASEAN.

Mr Shorten will have greater licence and does intend to once more venture into central and north Queensland .

Since last year's election, Labor has made a considerable effort to target federal seats in the area including Capricornia, Flynn, Dawson and Leichhardt, all Coalition held, some with a strong One Nation vote. It focuses on worker issues such as job security, penalty rates, Medicare, skills and training, and other themes which resonate.

Labor has held all four seats in recent years. In early October, Mr Shorten made his sixth visit to the area since the election.

"We want these seats in our column and we're going to show that we're prepared to put in the hard yards, not just rock up every three years," said a Labor spokesman at the time.

Labor strategists say Mr Shorten and his senior shadow ministers have established themselves in the region by being frequent visitors, meaning if they show up during the campaign, their presence would not be viewed with the same degree of cynicism should Mr Turnbull suddenly appear. On Monday, Deputy Labor leader Tanya Plibersek, so often derided by Barnaby Joyce as an inner-city basket weaver, was in Rockhampton, in the hear of Capricornia, helping the Labor candidate.

Ironically, hampering the Queensland Liberal National Party's efforts to take push back at the One Nation threat is the December 2 federal byelection for Mr Joyce's seat of New England. Mr Joyce would have been used in central and north Queensland to help campaign for LNP leader Tim Nicholls in these areas.

But he confirmed he would not be leaving New England for the campaign, even though he is an unbackable favourite to win, following decisions by all key rivals - Tony Windsor, One Nation and the Shooters and Fishers Party - not to contest.

Leaving his seat to venture into Queensland would be viewed as an act of hubris and he is prepared to leave nothing to chance.

Senator Hanson is in India and will return to campaign in Queensland. She was aware of the rampant speculation around federal Parliament last week that the Queensland election was about to be called but chose to go anyway on a one week Parliamentary delegation.

The Queensland election helped drive One Nation's decision to pull out of New England given Senator Hanson, the party's key campaign weapon, needed to devote all her time in the party's heartland state where it is contesting 60 of the 93 seats. One Nation was never going to win New England anyway, where its anti-establishment messages do not work against Mr Joyce.

The Coalition strategist noted that in the absence of Mr Joyce, the next best federal figure who could help out in the fight would be Tony Abbott but he acknowledged that could have incendiary consequences. Mr Abbott is in New York, where he is speaking to an anti-homosexual Christian group about gay marriage. Nationals Senator Matt Canavan, who has rejoined the ministry after being cleared by the High Court, is likely to help campaign for the state LNP in regional Queensland, He will press hard on the Adani coal mine and other energy issues.

One source said it was a short campaign and the impact of federal visits should not be taken too seriously.

HEADLINE: ACCC flags write-down of $50b NBN
SUBHEAD: Full cost recovery driving up prices, complaints
TEXT:
The competition regulator has urged the federal government to rescue NBN Co, by either writing down its value so it can charge lower prices, offering relief on its debt repayments, or paying for hard-to-connect households directly through budget handouts.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission recommended the Turnbull government "consider whether NBN Co should continue to be obliged to recover its full cost of investment through its prices", in a draft report on the communications sector released yesterday.

NBN Co currently collects an average $43 a month from retail service providers for each home they sell in to, but needs $52 just to recover costs, let alone fulfil the government's expectations of a 3 per cent annualised return on its $50 billion investment in the network.

The ACCC's report flags three options for bridging that gap: direct budget funding arrangements for non-commercial services, relief from having to repay debt provided by the government, or an asset write-down.

"We note that private sector firms that fail to meet rate of return targets regularly write down the carrying value of their assets," the draft report said.

Crucially, a write-down would give NBN Co breathing space to reduce its access and bandwidth charges to retail telcos, which the ACCC partly blames for the 159 per cent rise in complaints against the NBN lodged by the telco ombudsman in 2016-17. The regulator's interviews with consumers revealed many felt their internet speeds were slower than the ADSL or cable broadband connections that the NBN had forced them off, even when they were paying higher monthly charges.

But the government is unmoved by calls to spend any more taxpayer money on the NBN since it lent it a further $19.5 billion last November, which was meant to cover completion of the rollout and be repaid in 2020-21.

Treasurer Scott Morrison yesterday played down fears the government could suffer a budget hit if the NBN wrote down its valuation, saying the network's earnings have "actually improved over the last two years; it's not got worse".

Challenged on whether the government could expect the returns from NBN it had been anticipating, Mr Morrison told Sky News Business it had not received advice to the contrary.

On whether there might need to be a write-down, Mr Morrison said the decision would be one for the company and not the government.

"That is a decision that is actually taken by the NBN in terms of how they're looking forward and the assumptions they're making. There is no suggestion at the moment that there would be any change to that."

The ACCC draft report recommends that despite objections from Telstra and Optus, NBN Co should be encouraged to improve access to its wholesale network for smaller retail players as a way of driving down prices.

"We think there could be a transitional role for NBN Co to provide a targeted aggregation service to smaller providers to support their entry and expansion during the rollout period," ACCC chairman Rod Sims said.

The report noted that while 10 per cent of mobile phone plans in Australia were bought through "mobile virtual network operators" with no network of their own, the penetration of retailers piggybacking off the NBN backhaul of major telcos was only 4 per cent.

The ACCC rejected NBN chief Bill Morrow's call for a levy on wireless competitors. Fixed-line competitors to the NBN will from July 2018 have to pay a levy starting at $7.09 a month to help subsidise delivery to hard-to-connect customers.

Mr Morrow had suggested that levy be extended to wireless customers, but the ACCC disagrees.

"While wireless substitution may affect the ability of NBN Co to recover its costs, the ACCC does not see a case for regulation that constrains this competition with the NBN," Mr Sims said.

The regulator has agreed with NBN Co in pointing some blame for the high level of dissatisfied customers - about 15 per cent of those connected to the NBN to date - at retailers not buying enough network capacity.

More than half the retailers it surveyed were not passing on bulk discounts for network capacity - or "connectivity virtual circuit" (CVC) - which NBN Co introduced in June.

The ACCC is also worried that relatively expensive CVC prices are creating an incentive for retailers to compete on price rather than speed, noting that Telstra faces little competition at the premium end of the market.

Mr Sims will hold off using his veto power over NBN pricing, pending the government-owned telco's ongoing industry consultation.

"We would prefer an industry-led solution, and we have delayed our decision on NBN Co's Special Access Undertaking to facilitate this."

Telstra's relatively clear run at the premium, 100mbps end of the NBN market is getting unfair assistance from a far older part of the telecommunications landscape, argued Vodafone chief strategy officer Dan Lloyd.

He said the universal service obligation, a deal under which Telstra was subsidised by taxpayers, as well as telcos like Vodafone, to ensure phone access to everybody in Australia, was anachronistic at a time when the NBN rollout and expanding mobile coverage would soon see more than 99 per cent of people connected.

"Government data shows that there is an anti-competitive subsidy of around $150 million a year flowing to the largest and most profitable telco at the expense of its competitors and taxpayers," Mr Lloyd said. "Alarm bells are ringing over this arrangement but the ACCC fails to question it."

HEADLINE: Westpac takes on ASIC alone over rate rigging
TEXT:
Westpac Banking Corp is expected to tell the Federal Court on Tuesday that 12 of the 16 contraventions alleged by the corporate regulator for rigging the bank bill swap rate have no merit whatsoever and the corporate regulator has taken the rest of their traders' conversations out of context.

ANZ Banking Group and National Australia Banking Group confirmed their settlements with the regulator to the court on Monday, but Westpac is fighting on alone in a trial to begin on Tuesday and expected to run until Christmas.

Based on NAB's $50 million settlement confirmed on Friday evening - where NAB agreed it "attempted to engage in unconscionable conduct" on 12 occasions from ASIC's original claim of 50 contraventions - Westpac faces just 16 alleged contraventions and could potentially settle the case, estimated to have cost ASIC and the banks more than $80 million in legal fees, for as little as $5 million. But Westpac CEO Brian Hartzer and chairman Lindsay Maxsted are said to have personally examined ASIC's case and at this stage are determined to fight it.

The ANZ and NAB settlements clear the way for Philip Crutchfield, QC, who made his name working with Robert Richter, QC, defending Steve Vizard and defending Richard Pratt against the competition regulator, to open ASIC's case with the conversations of senior trader Col "The Rat" Roden expected to take centre stage.

"I know it's completely wrong but ... but f--- it I may as well, we've got so much money on it," one taped conversation of Roden reveals.

As with other conversations, Westpac claims this conversation has been misinterpreted and Mr Roden was referring to his perception that the level of the BBSW was "wrong" given the RBA was scheduled to meet that day and potentially move interest rates, which Mr Roden believed was being mis-priced in the markets.

A further conversation presented by ASIC to support its allegations took place on April 6, 2010, in which Mr Roden boasted he had made "$12 million bucks". Westpac claims this sum related to revaluations on its book, which was "exposed to domestic interest rates due to the increase in the RBA cash rate" and not profits related to the movement of the BBSW. The RBA lifted the cash rate from 4 per cent to 4.25 per cent on that day. Westpac will also make much of a conversation, presented by ASIC to support its claim against Westpac, between Mr Roden and a Reserve Bank official, Matt Boge, identified only as "Matt" in ASIC's filing.

In that conversation, Mr Roden discussed how "f------ with the rate set" could hurt some customers and ultimately and "deservedly" harm the bank's reputation if an inquiry into the bank bill market was ever conducted. But Westpac argues the comments were "in response to a general inquiry by Mr Boge into anomalous trading he was observing from other market participants and ... the reason for the current disparity in pricing" between bank bills and futures contracts.

Westpac will also argue at one point in time Westpac would have made only $118,000 from a one basis point fall in the BBSW, even though it had spent $1.6 billion buying bank bills. Westpac says because the benefit was so small it could not have been acting with a "dominant purpose" to manipulate the market, the test the law requires ASIC to meet to win its case.

On Monday, Justice Jonathan Beach referred the ANZ and NAB settlements to federal court judge Jane Jagot on November 10 to be signed off.

"The parties ASIC and ANZ have now completed the in-principle agreement of which we informed the court last week," ANZ counsel Alan Archibald, QC, told the court on Monday.

NAB's counsel Neil Young, QC, also confirmed its deal, which was announced to the ASX late on Friday. "ASIC and NAB have executed a settlement agreement ... and like ANZ, your Honour, we would seek an order referring our case to another judge for the purpose of the penalty hearing," he said.

But ASIC confirmed negotiations with Westpac had been fruitless. "If the court pleases, that matter is proceeding, your honour," Mr Crutchfield for ASIC told the court.

NAB announced details of its settlement, flagged by The Australian Financial Review last Monday, late on Friday evening on a heavy day for news during which five MPs, including deputy Prime Minister Barnaby Joyce, were ruled ineligible to sit in Parliament.

Although the details of the deal are yet to be ratified by the court, NAB was facing 50 alleged contraventions but ultimately admitted to 12 breaches and confirmed its settlement would include a $50 million payment, which included a $10 million penalty, $20 million to cover the legal costs of ASIC and a $20 million donation.

Last week, the Financial Review broke the news that ANZ had reached agreement on a settlement with the regulator minutes before the case was due to begin, estimated to be worth around $50 million. ANZ announced a $6.9 billion profit last Thursday with NAB set to present their annual results on Thursday and Westpac on Monday.

Justice Jonathan Beach is not ruling out the prospect that Westpac could still settle before the trial kicks off on Tuesday or before next Friday when Justice Jagot will hear the ANZ and NAB settlement deals.

"If the Westpac matter resolves itself I may deal with all cases and all penalty issues," the judge said. "I congratulate the parties in each of the ANZ and NAB proceedings for their hard work in getting to this stage."

While Commonwealth Bank is facing hundreds of millions of dollars in penalties from AUSTRAC, which has launched legal proceedings alleging 53,700 breaches of the anti-money laundering laws, on Friday ASIC confirmed it is still within the statute of limitation to bring BBSW proceedings against CBA.

"We will need to consider our position. We have not formed a view yet," ASIC commissioner Cathie Armour told a parliamentary hearing on Friday.

HEADLINE: Why it pays to hang on to the older workers
TEXT:
Employers should ramp up efforts to hire and retain older workers because they are more likely to remain loyal and less inclined to quit because they believe the grass is greener elsewhere, research suggests.

According to analysis of official labour market data by the Parliamentary Library, even though companies fire more workers over the age of 45, they may be better served keeping them in a job.

Workers under the age of 34, by comparison, are twice as likely to leave a job because they want a change of scene, or anticipate finding a better job or conditions.

The figures underscore the shifting and, at times, contradictory signals emerging from the national labour market, which has been on a tear over the past year, even as measures of "under-employment" remain elevated.

Treasurer Scott Morrison said on Monday that he remained confident the jobs market would eventually generate the wages growth that workers and the government were counting on.

While he acknowledged that last week's weak inflation figures - partly driven by a lack of wages pressures - were "at the lower end of my expectations", Mr Morrison said the Reserve Bank of Australia would continue to take that into account.

He noted on Sky News Business that the fading impact of the mining investment boom - a period he said saw wages get ahead of productivity - meant the labour market was "coming back into sync again".

Policy makers both in Australia and abroad are being confounded by an unusual combination of strong jobs growth at the same time as weak wages.

Deputy Reserve Bank governor Guy Debelle said last week there was still a "sizeable degree" of spare capacity in the labour market, and warned Australia might suffer the same advanced economy affliction of a breakdown between hiring and pay packets.

According to the Parliamentary Library research, based on surveys of people who worked in the 12 months ended February 2017, while there were differences between men and women on the main reason they left a job, the top cause was the search for something better.

About 23 per cent of men and 19 per cent of women left a job because they wanted a better one.

Retrenchment was more likely to hit men than women - 19 per cent compared with 13 per cent - whereas women were more likely to cite family reason for leaving, 16 per cent versus 6 per cent.

Among young workers aged 15 to 19 years, 22 per cent were most likely to leave a job because it was temporary or seasonal, while one in five aged 20 to 24 left for greener pastures.

People aged 25 to 34 years and 35 to 44 were most likely to leave a job for family reasons, which encompassed reasons such as marrying, having children, caring for others, holidaying, moving house or having a spouse who was transferred.

The main reason people aged 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 years left their jobs was due to their own ill health or injury.

Key points

Workers under 34 are twice as likely to leave a job because of a change of scene.

23 per cent of men and 19 per cent of women leave a job wanting a better one.

HEADLINE: Lander & Rogers faces harassment claims by gay former partner
TEXT:
National mid-tier law firm Lander & Rogers is fighting a former partner over the allegation he was sexually harassed at work because he is openly gay.

Former Sydney-based fixed-share partner Craig Higginbotham has filed a complaint in the Australian Human Rights Commission alleging he was sexually harassed at work because he is a gay man and victimised because he complained about it to equity partners Greg McKenzie and Jonathan Quilty.

Lander & Rogers denies these allegations and says Mr Higginbotham was sacked because he repeatedly breached the partnership agreement by working as a real estate agent and doing legal work without notifying the firm.

Mr Higginbotham alleges another fixed-share partner in Sydney's commercial disputes team, Tean Kerr, logged onto his computer at work and sent inappropriate emails to the team from Mr Higginbotham's account.

Mr Kerr also allegedly sent Mr Higginbotham a calendar invite called "Queer Eye for the Straight Guy", in reference to a reality television show, after the pair decided to take a newest team member shopping for a new suit. He also made disparaging comments about Mr Higginbotham's practice in an effort to undermine his confidence.

Between 2015 and early 2017, Mr Higginbotham claims he complained about Mr Kerr's conduct and his treatment of a female senior associate in his team on multiple occasions to Mr McKenzie, and later Mr Quilty, but Mr McKenzie allegedly told Mr Higginbotham not to involve HR and told him to ignore the behaviour.

In March, the firm sent him a "show cause" letter asking him to explain his involvement as a real estate agent with a company known as East West - Business and Property.

Mr Higginbotham filed a sexual harassment claim with the commission two weeks later. His partnership was terminated in April after the equity partners found he spent significant time during business hours working for East West's business associates, including doing legal work without charging the clients on behalf of the firm.

The firm says Mr Higginbotham did not complain about sexual harassment and discrimination until he was sent the show cause letter. It also says he participated in some of the joking emails.

In June, Mr Higginbotham was ordered by the Federal Court to pay the firm's costs on an indemnity basis and was referred to the NSW legal services commissioner to determine if he filed misleading and untruthful evidence.

Mr Higginbotham had applied to the Federal Court for an interlocutory injunction in May to stop the partners expelling him from the partnership, but did not disclose a material piece of evidence, namely he had a job offer from another firm. The application has been discontinued and he now works for boutique law firm Teneo Legal.

In a statement to The Australian Financial Review, Mr Higginbotham said: "I trusted the senior partners to take action but in the end it was swept under the carpet and the conduct continued. I have worked in a number of law firms for over 26 years and never in that time did I experience such a toxic, discriminatory, work environment."

Chief executive partner Andrew Wilder said: "Mr Higginbotham breached numerous provisions of the partnership agreement, including involvement in real estate transactions as an agent, leaving us with no choice. The firm gave Mr Higginbotham every opportunity to respond to the breaches notified to him in a show cause letter, but he failed to provide substantive responses."

Mr Wilder says the suggestion Mr Higginbotham was dismissed because he is gay or made a complaint is "ridiculous" and says the firm does pro bono work with the LGBTIQ community and is a signatory to the marriage equality campaign.

The Australian Financial Review understands Lander & Rogers has settled three cases with a former partner and two employees in recent years because the individuals had complained about HR issues. Mr Wilder said the firm believes it has acted correctly in "less than a handful of cases we have had to deal with in the past".

HEADLINE: Petra hires Deutsche trader
TEXT:
Deutsche Bank research sales trader Neil Watson has left the bank, sources told Street Talk on Monday.

It is understood Watson, who serviced hedge fund clients and small-cap fund managers at the German bank, has been hired by stockbroker Petra Capital.

Watson, a former geophysicist, spent five years at Deutsche and also worked as an equity analyst at Credit Suisse and BNP Paribas.

Sydney-based Petra has seen something of an exodus in recent months. Staff exits have included director Michael Henshaw, who led the firm's corporate coverage for a number of big clients including TPG Telecom, in July.

At the time, sources said George Marias-owned Petra, which has about 25 staff, was actively recruiting.

Elsewhere, and as first reported by this column on Monday, UBS has poached Goldman Sachs' senior research analyst Nathan Reilly.

Street Talk understands Reilly, who covered industrials and was head of construction and infrastructure research, resigned from the US-based firm after a decade. He joined Goldman after various stints in the accounting profession, according to LinkedIn.

Reilly replaces former UBS industrial materials analyst Ramoun Lazar, who resigned in August to join the buyside at the Macquarie High Conviction Fund.

HEADLINE: Chocolatier Godiva has a taste for Australia roll-out
TEXT:
Luxury chocolatier Godiva is plotting a foray into the Australian market, shaking off sombre official numbers for retail sales.

Street Talk understands the group's plans are well advanced with more than 10 stores in the works over the medium term. A site in Melbourne for the first opening has already been secured in the Emporium centre.

The moves by Godiva, part of Ulker Group which is owned by Turkish giant Yildiz Holding, show high-end brands still have a strong interest in the Australian market.

In another part of that market a recent example is premium handbag maker Furla agreeing to buy back its local stores earlier this year.

Godiva owns and operates more than 450 boutiques and shops worldwide in more than 80 countries. In Australia, the chocolates and related products are available only in David Jones premium food courts.

The timing is interesting, though, with the first Godiva local store and cafe opening expected before the year's end.

The latest data showed retail sales had their biggest two-month decline in seven years as debt-laden households clamped down on restaurants, cafes and food shopping. The numbers were for July and August.

Also, Godiva, under a different guise, had a false start in Australia in 2009 when it briefly opened a store and cafe in the international terminal of Sydney Airport. That didn't survive.

Once up and running the group will go head-to-head here with the likes of Max Brenner, Guylian cafes and Haigh's Chocolates.

It comes as prospective buyers of high-profile confectionery brand Darrell Lea get toward the pointy end of a sale process for the company.
